**"Pathétique" Symphony (Symphony No. 6 in B minor)**
Tchaikovsky's last symphony, premiered in 1893 just nine days before his death, possibly by suicide. It opens with a low bassoon melody in E minor, has a first-movement bassoon passage marked with six p's (pppppp), and ends unusually with a slow "Adagio lamentoso" finale whose melody alternates between the first and second violins.

**"Limping waltz" in 5/4 time**
The second movement (Allegro con grazia) of the Pathétique Symphony is a waltz written in 5/4 instead of the usual 3/4, giving it a lopsided, "limping" feel. It is the single most common clue in Tchaikovsky questions.

**1812 Overture**
Tchaikovsky's 1880 orchestral work commemorating Russia's defeat of Napoleon's invasion, including the Battle of Borodino. "La Marseillaise" represents the French army and is drowned out by the Russian anthem "God Save the Tsar," and the score calls for church bells and real cannon fire.

**Symphony No. 4 in F minor and the "Fate" motif**
This symphony opens with a powerful brass fanfare on A-flat representing Fate, inspired by Beethoven, which returns in the finale. Its second movement is an "Andantino in modo di canzona" with a melancholy oboe melody, its scherzo has the strings play pizzicato throughout, and its finale quotes the folk song "In the Field Stood a Birch Tree." It was dedicated to his patron Nadezhda von Meck.

**Piano Concerto No. 1 in B-flat minor**
Opens with a fortissimo French horn fanfare and crashing D-flat major piano chords. It was originally meant for Nikolai Rubinstein, who harshly criticized it before later reconsidering, and Van Cliburn's 1958 performance of it won the first International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow.

**Swan Lake**
Ballet in which the sorcerer von Rothbart turns Odette into a swan by day, and Prince Siegfried is tricked into pledging his love to Rothbart's daughter Odile, the "Black Swan," who is disguised as Odette. Lev Ivanov choreographed its "Dance of the Little Swans," in which four dancers move with their hands linked.

**The Nutcracker**
Christmas ballet in which Clara (or Marie) helps the Nutcracker defeat the Mouse King and travels to the Land of Sweets. It features the celesta in the "Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy," the "Waltz of the Flowers," and national dances such as the Spanish chocolate dance and the Russian Trepak, with its squatting prisiadka kicks.

**The Sleeping Beauty**
Ballet (Op. 66) in which Princess Aurora pricks her finger on a spindle given by the wicked fairy Carabosse and falls into a cursed sleep until Prince Désiré awakens her. It features the difficult "Rose Adagio," in which four suitors bring Aurora roses, and its waltz was adapted as "Once Upon a Dream" in Disney's Sleeping Beauty.

**Eugene Onegin**
Tchaikovsky's opera based on Pushkin's verse novel about the daughters of Madame Larina. Tatyana pours out her love for Onegin in the "Letter Scene," the Frenchman Triquet sings couplets in her honor, and the poet Lensky is killed by Onegin in a duel. Tchaikovsky's other operas include The Queen of Spades, also from Pushkin, and Iolanta.

**Romeo and Juliet Overture-Fantasy**
Tchaikovsky's tone poem on Shakespeare's play, written at the urging of Mily Balakirev, who also convinced him to revise it. Its sweeping "love theme" is one of the most famous melodies in classical music.

**Symphony No. 5 in E minor**
Opens with a melancholy motto theme in the low clarinets (long G, two short Gs, long A) that recurs throughout and returns triumphantly in major at the start of the finale. Its second movement contains a famous D major horn solo in 12/8 time.

**Capriccio Italien**
An orchestral fantasy inspired by Tchaikovsky's 1880 stay in Rome. It opens with a trumpet fanfare imitating the bugle call he heard every day from a cavalry barracks near his hotel.

**Serenade for Strings and Mozartiana**
Both works honor Tchaikovsky's love of Mozart. The C major Serenade for Strings opens with a "Pezzo in forma di sonatina" and includes a waltz and an élégie, while his fourth orchestral suite, Mozartiana, orchestrates Mozart pieces including Liszt's transcription of Ave verum corpus and the Variations on a Theme by Gluck.

**Piano Trio in A minor**
A two-movement trio "dedicated to the memory of a great artist," Nikolai Rubinstein, who died in 1881. The opening "Pezzo elegiaco" is followed by a long set of variations that ends by returning to the funereal opening theme.

**"Little Russian" Symphony (Symphony No. 2)**
Tchaikovsky's second symphony, nicknamed for its use of Ukrainian folk songs, including "Down by Mother Volga" in a solo horn and "The Crane" in its finale. His other named symphonies include No. 1 "Winter Dreams," No. 3 "Polish," and the Manfred Symphony, based on Lord Byron's poem.
